To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the development of nonarteric ischemic optic neuropaths (NAION) and glaucomas is correlated with nocturnal hypotensive episodes, and that these episodes are more frequent in hypertensive patients who are taking antihypertensive drugs, particularly beta-blockers, at night.

nocturnal arterial hypoten-sion (particularly nocturnal systolic arterial hypotension) plays a significant role in the development and progression in nonarteric anterior is-chemic optic neuropathy (NAION), glaucomat-ous optic neuropathy, and central retinal ve-nous occlusion.

nocturnal arterial hypotenension (particularly in hypertensive patients on oral antihypertensive therapy) is associated with an increased risk of glaucomatouss optic neuropathy, nonarteric anterior optic neuropathy, retinal vein occlusion, and central retinal vein occlusions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the pathophysiology of the development and progression and of the treatment of glaucomatousoptic neuropathy and nonarteric anterior optic neuropathy.
the pathogenesis of ocular disorders associated with systemic arterial hypertension and the role of nocturnal arterial hypertension in their development.

the role of nocturnal arterial hypertension in the development of a variety of ocualr disorders, including nonarteric anterior optic neuropathy, glaucomatousoptic neuropathy, and central retinal artery occlusion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
arterial hypertension and arterial hypotensive treatment are not mutually exclusive, and that both are important factors in the pathophysiology of ocular and optic neuropathy.

the development and/or progression of ocular manifestations (including nonarteric ischemic optic neuropathies, glaucomatousoptical neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion, and central retinal vein occlusion) in systemic arterial hypertensive patients may be due to a combined effect of systemic arterial hypertension, which is a predisposing factor, and nocturnal arterial hypotenension, which is a causative factor.

the development of occlusive vascular disorders of the optic nerve head and retina are not only related to arterial hypertension but to arterial hypotension as well, particularly nocturnal arterial hypotenstion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ophthalmologist must be aware that nocturnal hypotensive therapy is not always beneficial and may be harmful to the patient. (Am J Ophthalmol 1997;123:736-47.)
arterial hypertension and arterial hypotensive drugs can be a double-edged sword.
the ophthalmologist and the treating physician should be aware that arterial hypotension may be as important a cause of ocular or optic neuropathies as arterial hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of ocu-lar and optic nerve head ischemia is more likely related to arterial hypotension than to arterial hypertension.
arterial hypotension is a risk factor for ocular ischemic disorders.
arterial hypertension and nocturnal hypotensión are both important risk factors for the development of ocu-lar or optic nerve head disorders.
